title: Bronze statuette of Herakles
description: An Italic representation of the hero. The museum places it among statuettes showing Herakles advancing with club and bow; it does not identify a particular labour.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of Herakles, bronze. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Marble relief fragment with scenes from the Trojan War
description: This small relief belongs to the tabulae iliacae, which depict Trojan War scenes. The museum identifies a signature by Theodoros on the reverse. It documents Roman engagement with the story, not an event from the war.
imageAlt: Marble relief fragment with scenes from the Trojan War, palombino marble. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Perseus with the Head of Medusa
creator: Antonio Canova
description: Canova's sculpture presents Perseus holding Medusa's head. Made in the early nineteenth century, it shows the myth's later artistic reception rather than an ancient depiction.
imageAlt: Perseus with the Head of Medusa, marble. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Statuette of Osiris
description: This figure shows Osiris in mummy form with the crook and flail of kingship. It provides evidence for his representation in Egyptian religious art, rather than depicting the full account of his death and restoration.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of Osiris with a tall crown and arms crossed over the torso. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Foundation figure of Ur-Namma holding a basket
description: The inscription identifies this figure with a temple of Inanna built or restored by Ur-Namma. It shows the ruler, not Inanna, and provides context for her worship rather than illustrating her descent to the underworld.
imageAlt: Copper-alloy foundation figure of a man holding a basket above his head. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Ibeji Twin Figure
creator: Yoruba artist
description: The museum connects ere ibeji figures with care for a deceased twin. This object supports the page’s discussion of remembrance; it is not evidence for the origin episode formerly published here.
imageRights: Image reuse not established; view at museum

title: Terracotta hydria (water jar)
description: A South Italian water jar whose painted frieze the museum tags as showing Hecate alongside Zeus, Athena, Aphrodite, and Eros. It documents her place among the Olympian company in fourth-century Apulian vase painting.
imageAlt: Terracotta hydria with a painted mythological frieze including Hecate. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Rama and Lakshmana Search in Vain for Sita: Illustrated folio from a dispersed Ramayana series
medium: Ink and opaque watercolor on paper
description: A Rajasthani manuscript illustration from a dispersed Ramayana series showing Rama and Lakshmana searching for Sita after her abduction. It reflects the story's reception in Mewar court painting rather than an ancient attestation.
imageAlt: Illustrated folio showing Rama and Lakshmana searching a forest landscape for Sita. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: The Combat of Rama and Ravana
description: A painted and dyed cotton hanging from the Coromandel Coast depicting the battle between Rama and Ravana. The museum's own title names both figures directly.
imageAlt: Textile hanging showing the combat of Rama and Ravana with armies in battle. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: The Demon Marichi Tries to Dissuade Ravana; Illustrated folio from a dispersed Ramayana series
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, silver, and gold on paper
description: A Kangra-school folio from a dispersed Ramayana series showing the demon Marichi trying to talk Ravana out of his plan. The museum's title names Ravana explicitly as the recipient of the advice.
imageAlt: Illustrated folio showing the demon Marichi speaking with Ravana. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Cult Image of the God Ptah
description: A lapis lazuli statuette identified by the museum as a cult image of Ptah, shown in his standard mummiform pose holding a staff. Small images like this were placed in shrines or temples as votive offerings.
imageAlt: Lapis lazuli statuette of the mummiform god Ptah holding a staff. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Ptah
description: A cast metal statuette the museum catalogs simply as Ptah, showing the god's characteristic close-fitting cap and mummiform body. Votive figures of this type were mass-produced for temple donation in the Late Period.
imageAlt: Cupreous metal statuette of the god Ptah in mummiform pose. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Amun
description: A cast metal statuette the museum identifies simply as Amun, wearing the god's characteristic tall plumed crown. Figures like this were dedicated at temples as personal acts of devotion.
imageAlt: Cupreous metal statuette of the god Amun wearing a tall plumed crown. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Statuette of Amun
description: A gold statuette of Amun standing in a striding pose, tagged by the museum as depicting the god by name. Gold examples like this were rarer and costlier votive or funerary offerings than the more common bronze figures.
imageAlt: Gold statuette of the god Amun standing in a striding pose. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Head of the god Amun
description: A granodiorite head from a statue of Amun, dated by the museum to the years after the Amarna Period when his cult was restored to prominence. The scale of the stone points to an original temple statue rather than a personal votive.
imageAlt: Granodiorite head from a temple statue of the god Amun. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bes amulet
description: A faience amulet of the dwarf god Bes, tagged by the museum with his name. Bes amulets were worn for protection, especially of households, women in childbirth, and children.
imageAlt: Faience amulet in the form of the protective dwarf god Bes. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Magical Stela with Horus the Child
description: The Metternich Stela, a magical healing stela carved with spells against venomous bites; the museum tags it with figures including Bes and Horus the Child, whose image dominates the front. Owners would pour water over the inscribed surface and drink the water as a cure.
imageAlt: Carved stone healing stela (the Metternich Stela) showing Horus the Child flanked by protective deities including Bes. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Papyrus fragment with a painting of Khepri, Shu, Tefnut, Thoth, and Isis in a solar boat
description: A fragment from a funerary papyrus painted with a scene of deities in a solar boat; the museum's own title lists Shu among the figures depicted, alongside Khepri, Tefnut, Thoth, and Isis.
imageAlt: Painted papyrus fragment showing deities including Shu riding in a solar boat. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Cowroid with Outward-facing Merged Lions and Sun Disk
description: A glazed steatite cowroid seal whose inscription and design the museum catalogs as invoking Re, Shu, and Tefnut alongside a sun disk and lions. It served as an amuletic seal rather than a temple image.
imageAlt: Glazed steatite cowroid seal-amulet naming the gods Re, Shu, and Tefnut. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Cast reconstruction of Babylonian Flood Tablet
description: A nineteenth-century plaster cast reproducing the Babylonian Flood Tablet, the Gilgamesh Epic tablet in which Utnapishtim recounts surviving the great flood. The cast documents how the deciphered tablet circulated among museums after its 1872 translation, not an ancient depiction of Utnapishtim himself.
imageAlt: Plaster cast reproduction of the cuneiform Flood Tablet from the Epic of Gilgamesh. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta column-krater (vase for mixing wine and water)
description: An Attic column-krater whose painted scene the museum tags as including Zeus among other figures. Large mixing vessels like this were used at the symposium, the Greek drinking party where mythological imagery was common.
imageAlt: Terracotta column-krater with a painted scene including Zeus. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta Nolan neck-amphora (jar)
description: An Attic neck-amphora whose painted figure the museum's record tags as Zeus, together with a bow and arrow, an unusual attribute for him. Nolan amphorae like this were a favored shape for single mythological figures in the Classical period.
imageAlt: Terracotta neck-amphora with a painted scene of Zeus. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Marble sarcophagus with the contest between the Muses and the Sirens
description: Fragments of a Roman marble sarcophagus carved with the contest between the Muses and the Sirens; the museum's tags list Hera among the figures on the surrounding frieze. The relief shows how Greek mythological subjects continued to furnish Roman funerary art centuries later.
imageAlt: Fragments of a marble sarcophagus with a relief frieze including a figure of Hera. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of a god, possibly Poseidon
description: A Hellenistic bronze statuette the museum identifies as possibly depicting Poseidon, shown in a striding pose that would originally have held an attribute such as a trident. The tentative identification reflects how sea deities and river gods shared similar iconography.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of a striding god, possibly Poseidon. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta hydria: kalpis (water jar)
description: An Attic water jar painted with a scene the museum tags as showing Poseidon among seahorses. The imagery reflects his domain over the sea on a vessel shape used for carrying water.
imageAlt: Terracotta hydria with a painted scene of Poseidon and seahorses. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta kylix (drinking cup)
description: An Archaic Attic drinking cup painted with a battle scene the museum tags as including Poseidon among warriors, horses, and an Iliad-related subject. Poseidon's involvement in the Trojan War appears throughout the Iliad.
imageAlt: Terracotta kylix with a painted battle scene including Poseidon. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Athena
description: A Roman bronze statuette the museum catalogs simply as Athena, shown helmeted in her role as goddess of war and wisdom. Small bronzes like this circulated widely as household or votive images across the Roman world.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of the helmeted goddess Athena. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Athena flying her owl
description: A Classical Greek bronze statuette the museum titles as Athena flying her owl, her sacred bird and symbol of wisdom. The pairing of goddess and owl was one of her most recognizable attributes in Greek art.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of Athena with her owl in flight. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta Panathenaic prize amphora (jar)
description: An Archaic Panathenaic prize amphora, the type of vessel filled with olive oil and awarded to victors at the Panathenaic Games in Athens; the museum tags its painted side as showing Athena, the festival's patron goddess.
imageAlt: Terracotta Panathenaic prize amphora with a painted figure of Athena. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Apollo
description: A Classical Greek bronze statuette the museum catalogs as Apollo. Bronze figurines of the god were common votive gifts at his sanctuaries.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of the god Apollo. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Apollo
description: A Roman bronze statuette the museum titles as Apollo with a quiver, referencing his role as archer god. Roman households and shrines used small bronzes like this for private devotion.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of Apollo shown with a quiver. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Artemis
description: A Hellenistic bronze statuette the museum catalogs as Artemis, goddess of the hunt and wilderness. Figures of this type were common temple and household dedications.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of the goddess Artemis. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze bust of Artemis
description: A Roman bronze bust the museum identifies as Artemis. Portrait-style busts of deities were used as decorative fittings as well as objects of devotion.
imageAlt: Bronze bust of the goddess Artemis. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Marble statuette of Aphrodite
description: A Hellenistic Greek marble statuette the museum catalogs as Aphrodite. Small-scale marble statuettes of the goddess were popular for private display in the Hellenistic period.
imageAlt: Marble statuette of the goddess Aphrodite. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Marble statue of a crouching Aphrodite
description: A Roman marble statue the museum identifies as a crouching Aphrodite, a popular type derived from a lost Hellenistic original showing the goddess bathing. The crouching pose was copied widely across the Roman world.
imageAlt: Marble statue of Aphrodite in a crouching pose. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Hermes
description: A bronze statuette the museum catalogs as Hermes, messenger god and patron of travelers and trade. Its Greek-or-Roman dating reflects how the type continued across the transition between the two cultures.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of the god Hermes. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta jug in the form of Dionysos
description: A terracotta jug shaped as the head of Dionysos, tagged by the museum with his name. Vessels formed as deity heads were a specialty of Hellenistic pottery workshops.
imageAlt: Terracotta jug in the form of the head of Dionysos. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta column-krater (bowl for mixing wine and water)
description: An Archaic Attic mixing bowl painted with a scene the museum tags as showing Dionysos with maenads and satyrs, his usual retinue of ecstatic followers. Vessels of this shape mixed wine and water at the symposium, fitting for imagery of the wine god.
imageAlt: Terracotta column-krater with a painted scene of Dionysos, maenads, and satyrs. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Ten marble fragments of the Great Eleusinian Relief
description: Fragments of the Great Eleusinian Relief, a Roman marble copy of a lost Greek original; the museum's tags identify Demeter and Persephone among the figures. The relief reflects imagery from the Eleusinian Mysteries, the cult centered on Demeter and her daughter.
imageAlt: Marble relief fragments from the Great Eleusinian Relief showing Demeter and Persephone. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Jupiter Capitolinus
description: A Roman bronze statuette the museum titles as Jupiter Capitolinus, referencing the cult image of Jupiter enshrined on Rome's Capitoline Hill. Statuettes of this type reproduced the pose of the great temple statue for private worship.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of Jupiter Capitolinus. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Jupiter Capitolinus
description: A second Roman bronze statuette the museum titles as Jupiter Capitolinus, showing the same enthroned type associated with the god's Capitoline cult statue.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of Jupiter Capitolinus. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Neptune
description: A Roman bronze statuette the museum catalogs as Neptune, god of the sea. The figure's now-missing attribute would originally have been a trident.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of the god Neptune. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Neptune
creator: Severo Calzetta da Ravenna
description: A mid-sixteenth-century Italian bronze statuette by Severo Calzetta da Ravenna depicting Neptune. It reflects the Renaissance revival of classical sea-god imagery in collectors' bronzes, not an ancient cult image.
imageAlt: Renaissance bronze statuette of Neptune by Severo da Ravenna. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Minerva
description: A Roman bronze statuette the museum catalogs as Minerva, the Roman goddess of war and wisdom equated with Athena. Small bronzes of this kind were common household devotional objects.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of the goddess Minerva. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Minerva
creator: Benvenuto Cellini
description: A sixteenth-century Italian bronze statuette attributed to Benvenuto Cellini depicting Minerva. It belongs to the Renaissance fashion for small classical-style bronzes made for collectors rather than an ancient cult object.
imageAlt: Renaissance bronze statuette of Minerva attributed to Benvenuto Cellini. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Marble statue of Aphrodite, the so-called Venus Genetrix
description: A Roman marble statue of the so-called Venus Genetrix type, named by the museum in its own title. The type descends from a cult statue associated with Venus as ancestress of the Julian imperial line.
imageAlt: Marble statue of Venus of the Venus Genetrix type. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Mars
creator: François Briot
description: A bronze plaquette of about 1610 by the French goldsmith François Briot depicting Mars with shield and sword, tagged by the museum with the god's name. Plaquettes like this were decorative collectors' objects modeled on classical armed figures.
imageAlt: Bronze plaquette depicting Mars with shield and sword, by François Briot. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Isis with infant Horus
description: A bronze statuette showing Isis nursing the infant Horus, a widely produced devotional type from the Late Period onward. The museum's own title names both figures.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of Isis nursing the infant Horus. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Isis nursing Horus
description: A second bronze figure of Isis nursing Horus, one of the most common devotional images in later Egyptian religion. Such figures were placed in shrines by worshippers seeking the goddess's maternal protection.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of Isis nursing the infant Horus. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Horus falcon
description: A faience amulet in the form of the Horus falcon wearing the double crown, tagged by the museum with his name. Falcon amulets invoked Horus's protection and his association with kingship.
imageAlt: Faience amulet of the Horus falcon wearing the double crown. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Statue of Horus as a falcon protecting King Nectanebo II
description: A stone statue showing Horus as a falcon protecting King Nectanebo II, who stands beneath the god's wings. The museum's title identifies both the god and the specific king he shelters.
imageAlt: Stone statue of Horus as a falcon sheltering King Nectanebo II. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Anubis
description: A cast metal statuette the museum catalogs simply as Anubis, god of embalming and the dead, in his jackal-headed form. Such figures were dedicated by worshippers concerned with proper burial and the afterlife.
imageAlt: Cupreous metal statuette of the jackal-headed god Anubis. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Statue of Anubis as a recumbent canid
culture: Egyptian, End of Late Period–Ptolemaic Period
description: A limestone statue of Anubis as a recumbent canid, originally painted black, the color associated with fertile Nile silt and rebirth. Statues of this type guarded tombs and funerary equipment.
imageAlt: Limestone statue of Anubis as a recumbent black jackal. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Striding Thoth
description: A faience statuette the museum titles as Striding Thoth, shown in his ibis-headed form as god of writing and knowledge. Faience figures of Thoth were common votive gifts at his cult centers.
imageAlt: Faience statuette of the ibis-headed god Thoth striding forward. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Ibis-headed god, Thoth
description: A bronze statuette the museum identifies as the ibis-headed god Thoth. Thoth's ibis form referenced the bird's association with wisdom and the recording of knowledge.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of the ibis-headed god Thoth. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bastet
medium: Leaded bronze, precious metal and black bronze inlays
description: A bronze figure of Bastet inlaid with precious metal, catalogued by the museum under her name. Cat-headed images of Bastet were popular votive and household objects associating her with protection and fertility.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of the cat goddess Bastet with inlaid decoration. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bastet
description: A cast metal figure of Bastet, one of many produced in the Late and Ptolemaic Periods when her cult at Bubastis drew large numbers of pilgrims and votive offerings.
imageAlt: Cupreous metal statuette of the cat goddess Bastet. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Scarab Inscribed with a Blessing Related to Re
description: A green glazed steatite scarab inscribed with a blessing formula invoking Re. Scarabs like this were worn as amulets or used as seals, carrying the god's name rather than a figural image of him.
imageAlt: Glazed steatite scarab inscribed with a blessing formula naming the god Re. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Lion-Headed Goddess
description: A cast metal statuette of a lion-headed goddess the museum tags as Sekhmet, the fierce protector deity associated with war and healing. Bronze figures of Sekhmet were dedicated by worshippers seeking her dual powers of destruction and protection.
imageAlt: Cupreous metal statuette of the lion-headed goddess Sekhmet. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Lion-headed goddess
description: A second lion-headed goddess statuette tagged by the museum as Sekhmet, part of the large body of Late Period bronze votive figures dedicated to her.
imageAlt: Cupreous metal statuette of the lion-headed goddess Sekhmet. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Menat counterpoise with figures of Hathor as a woman and a cow
description: A menat counterpoise, the weight balancing a beaded ceremonial necklace used in Hathor's cult, cast with images of the goddess as both a woman and a cow. The museum's own title names Hathor directly.
imageAlt: Bronze menat counterpoise cast with figures of the goddess Hathor. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bronze statuette of Osiris
description: A second bronze statuette of Osiris in his mummiform pose, holding the crook and flail. Figures like this were among the most commonly dedicated votive bronzes in the Late Period, reflecting Osiris's central role in beliefs about the afterlife.
imageAlt: Bronze statuette of the mummiform god Osiris holding the crook and flail. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Vishnu
description: A gilded copper-alloy figure of Vishnu from Nepal's Kathmandu Valley, dated by inscription to 1105 CE. The museum catalogs it simply as Vishnu, standing in his four-armed form holding his usual attributes.
imageAlt: Gilt copper-alloy figure of the god Vishnu, dated 1105 CE. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Standing Vishnu
description: A Chola-period bronze of Vishnu standing in a formal frontal pose, cast in South India for temple processional use. Chola bronzes of this kind were carried in festival processions rather than kept fixed in a shrine.
imageAlt: Copper-alloy processional bronze of the standing god Vishnu. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Shiva as Lord of Dance (Nataraja)
description: A Chola bronze of Shiva as Nataraja, Lord of the Dance, encircled by a ring of flame. This is one of the most celebrated forms of Hindu bronze sculpture, cast for temple processions in South India.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of Shiva as Nataraja, Lord of the Dance, within a ring of flame. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Shiva Seated with Uma (Umamaheshvara)
description: A Pala-period bronze showing Shiva seated with his consort Uma, a form known as Umamaheshvara. It reflects the eastern Indian bronze-casting tradition centered in Bihar and Bengal.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of Shiva seated with Uma (Umamaheshvara). Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Krishna
description: A South Indian bronze portable idol the museum catalogs simply as Krishna, made for personal devotional use. Portable images like this were carried and dressed in household worship.
imageAlt: Bronze portable devotional idol of the god Krishna. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Yashoda with the Infant Krishna
culture: India (Tamil Nadu, Pudukkottai and Tanjavur districts)
description: A Chola bronze showing Krishna's foster mother Yashoda holding the infant Krishna, tagged by the museum with his name. The tender maternal subject was a popular one in South Indian temple bronzes.
imageAlt: Copper-alloy figure of Yashoda nursing the infant Krishna. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Seated Ganesha
description: A Thai bronze of a seated, elephant-headed Ganesha, tagged by the museum with his name. Ganesha's worship spread from India across Buddhist and Hindu Southeast Asia.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of the seated, elephant-headed god Ganesha. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Ganesha
description: A South Indian bronze figurine of Ganesha, part of the continuous tradition of casting the elephant-headed god for household and temple shrines.
imageAlt: Bronze figurine of the elephant-headed god Ganesha. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: The Goddess Durga Slaying Mahisha
description: A Nepali bronze the museum titles as the goddess Durga slaying Mahisha, the buffalo demon. The subject depicts her defining myth, in which she was created by the gods to defeat a demon none of them could kill alone.
imageAlt: Copper-alloy figure of the goddess Durga slaying the buffalo demon Mahisha. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Durga Mahishasura
description: A bronze figure the museum titles Durga Mahishasura, showing the goddess triumphing over the same buffalo demon. Images of this victory were widely produced across medieval India.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of the goddess Durga triumphing over the demon Mahishasura. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Hanuman Conversing
description: A Chola-period bronze the museum titles Hanuman Conversing, showing the monkey god in a gesture of speech. Hanuman's devotion to Rama made him one of the most widely worshipped figures from the Ramayana.
imageAlt: Copper-alloy figure of the monkey god Hanuman in conversation. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Seated Brahma
description: A Central Javanese bronze the museum titles Seated Brahma, showing the creator god enthroned on a lotus. It reflects the spread of Hindu bronze-casting traditions to Java.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of the seated creator god Brahma. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Brahma with Silver Eyes
description: A Javanese bronze the museum titles Brahma with Silver Eyes, its inlaid eyes a refinement typical of fine Central Javanese metalwork.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of the god Brahma with silver-inlaid eyes. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin)
medium: Wood (wiillow) with traces of pigment; single woodblock construction
description: A Yuan-dynasty wood sculpture the museum titles Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin), dated by inscription to 1282. Guanyin, the East Asian form of the bodhisattva of compassion, became one of the most widely venerated figures in Chinese Buddhism.
imageAlt: Wood sculpture of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin), dated 1282. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin)
description: A gilt bronze figure from the Five Dynasties period the museum titles Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin), an early example of the type before the fully Sinicized feminine form became standard.
imageAlt: Gilt bronze figure of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin). Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Luring the Sun Goddess Amaterasu Out of a Cave with Music; Death of the Historical Buddha
medium: Pair of hanging scrolls; ink, color, and gold on silk
description: A pair of Meiji-period hanging scrolls whose title the museum gives as Luring the Sun Goddess Amaterasu Out of a Cave with Music, depicting the myth in which the other gods coax her out of hiding to restore light to the world.
imageAlt: Hanging scroll depicting the sun goddess Amaterasu being lured from her cave. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: The God Izanagi and Goddess Izanami
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
description: An Edo-period hanging scroll the museum titles The God Izanagi and Goddess Izanami, depicting the primordial couple credited in Shinto myth with creating the islands of Japan.
imageAlt: Hanging scroll depicting the god Izanagi and goddess Izanami. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Fireman’s Jacket (Hikeshi-Banten) with Susanoo-no-mikoto Deity Scene
medium: Quilted cotton with tube-drawn paste-resist dyeing (tsutsugaki) with hand-painted details
description: A quilted cotton fireman's jacket dyed with a scene the museum titles as depicting Susanoo-no-mikoto. Edo-period firemen commissioned dramatic mythological and heroic scenes for the linings of their protective coats.
imageAlt: Fireman's jacket dyed with a scene of the deity Susanoo-no-mikoto. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: The Moon Goddess Chang E
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
description: A Ming-dynasty hanging scroll the museum titles The Moon Goddess Chang E, showing the goddess who, in the best-known version of her myth, drank an elixir of immortality and rose to live on the moon.
imageAlt: Hanging scroll depicting the moon goddess Chang E. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: The Monkey King Songokū, from the Chinese novel Journey to the West
medium: Woodblock print (surimono); ink and color on paper
description: A Japanese surimono print titled by the museum The Monkey King Songoku, from the Chinese novel Journey to the West, using the Japanese reading of Sun Wukong's name. It shows the Chinese Monkey King's story reaching Japanese print culture in the early nineteenth century.
imageAlt: Woodblock print of the Monkey King (Sun Wukong) from Journey to the West. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Chalchiuhtlicue
description: A Mexica (Aztec) basalt figure the museum catalogs simply as Chalchiuhtlicue, goddess of lakes, rivers, and running water. Stone images like this were carved in the century before the Spanish conquest.
imageAlt: Basalt figure of the water goddess Chalchiuhtlicue. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Head of a Water Deity (Chalchiuhtlicue)
description: A basalt head the museum titles Head of a Water Deity (Chalchiuhtlicue), broken from a larger figure of the Mexica water goddess.
imageAlt: Basalt head of the water goddess Chalchiuhtlicue. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Head from a figure, Xochipilli-Macuilxochitl
description: An obsidian head the museum titles Head from a figure, Xochipilli-Macuilxochitl, naming the Mexica flower prince associated with music, pleasure, and the arts, closely linked with the god Macuilxochitl.
imageAlt: Carved obsidian head from a figure of Xochipilli. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Cuneiform tablet: hymn to Marduk
description: A cuneiform clay tablet the museum catalogs as a hymn to Marduk, chief god of the Babylonian pantheon. The tablet is a textual rather than figural attestation of his worship.
imageAlt: Cuneiform clay tablet inscribed with a hymn to the god Marduk. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Marble stele (grave marker) with a youth and little girl, and a capital and finial in the form of a sphinx
description: An Archaic Attic grave stele topped by a small sphinx finial, tagged by the museum with the creature's name. Sphinxes were common protective figures on Greek funerary monuments.
imageAlt: Marble grave stele with a sphinx-form finial. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Sphinx of Amenhotep III, possibly from a Model of a Temple
medium: Faience, remains of a travertine (Egyptian alabaster) tenon
description: A faience sphinx bearing the name of Amenhotep III, possibly from a model temple. Egyptian sphinxes combined a lion's body with a royal human head to guard sacred sites.
imageAlt: Faience sphinx associated with King Amenhotep III. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Sphinx of Hatshepsut
description: A granite sphinx carved with the features of Queen Hatshepsut, one of the best-known royal sphinxes in the museum's Egyptian collection.
imageAlt: Granite sphinx bearing the face of Hatshepsut. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Sardonyx cameo fragment with Hercules tying up Cerberus
description: A sardonyx cameo fragment the museum titles Hercules Tying Up Cerberus, showing the hero's final labor of capturing the three-headed hound of the underworld.
imageAlt: Sardonyx cameo fragment showing Hercules restraining Cerberus. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta kylix: eye-cup (drinking cup)
description: An Archaic Attic eye-cup whose painted scene the museum tags with Theseus and the Minotaur, depicting the hero's slaying of the bull-headed creature in the labyrinth.
imageAlt: Terracotta eye-cup with a painted scene of Theseus and the Minotaur. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Terracotta skyphos (deep drinking cup)
description: A Classical Attic drinking cup painted with a scene the museum tags as Theseus and the Minotaur, part of the well-attested cycle of vase imagery around the myth.
imageAlt: Terracotta skyphos with a painted scene of Theseus and the Minotaur. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Standing Nagaraja (Serpent King)
description: A Gupta-period red sandstone figure the museum titles Standing Nagaraja (Serpent King), a divine serpent-being whose cobra hood rises behind his head.
imageAlt: Red sandstone figure of a standing Nagaraja, a serpent king. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Buddha Sheltered by a Naga
description: A Khmer bronze the museum titles Buddha Sheltered by a Naga, showing the multi-headed serpent Mucalinda protecting the meditating Buddha, a well-known episode from Buddhist legend.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of the Buddha sheltered by the hood of a naga. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Garuda Finial
description: A gilt bronze finial in the form of Garuda, the half-man, half-bird creature and mount of Vishnu, made in Thailand for architectural decoration.
imageAlt: Gilt bronze finial in the form of the bird-man Garuda. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Striding Garuda (The Royal Solar Bird)
description: A Thai bronze the museum titles Striding Garuda (The Royal Solar Bird), showing the creature in an active pose rather than as a static architectural ornament.
imageAlt: Bronze figure of a striding Garuda. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Mirror With the Design of a Nine-Tailed Fox
medium: Woodblock print (surimono); ink and color on paper
description: An Edo-period Japanese print the museum titles Mirror With the Design of a Nine-Tailed Fox, depicting the shapeshifting kitsune associated in folklore with trickery and transformation.
imageAlt: Woodblock print showing a mirror decorated with a nine-tailed fox. Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Tale of the Fox (Kitsune no sōshi)
medium: Handscroll: ink and color on paper
description: An illustrated Edo-period handscroll titled Tale of the Fox (Kitsune no soshi), a narrative built around a shapeshifting kitsune. The handscroll documents the fox's role as a recurring figure in Japanese storytelling.
imageAlt: Illustrated handscroll from the Tale of the Fox (Kitsune no soshi). Photograph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
